title: Alps murders: Luger in a lake gives hope for French cold case
description: Police investigating the unsolved murder of a British family in France 14 years ago have an unexpected new clue with the discovery of a Luger pistol i
body: Police investigating the unsolved murder of a British family in France 14 years ago have an unexpected new clue with the discovery of a Luger pistol in the waters of a nearby lake.One of the few certainties in the killings of Saad al-Hilli with his wife and mother-in-law – as well as a passing cyclist – is that they were shot through the head with a Luger model P06, a type used by the Swiss army until around 1960.Now France's cold case unit has confirmed the discovery of a Luger in Lake Annecy,  in the Alps, not far from the scene of the murders in September 2012.According to Marianne magazine, which broke the story, it was British tourists on 20 August who found the weapon lying in two metres of water.At first they thought it was a water pistol, but realised their mistake when they felt its weight.The discovery was made near the very camping site – Le Solitaire du Lac – where the al-Hillis were staying in their caravan, Marianne reported.Forensic experts are now examining the weapon, which has been badly damaged by its time under water, to see if it is indeed a P06 model.It is estimated that around 60,000 Luger P06s were manufactured. But the number of Luger pistols in general that were made is more like three million.Exhaustive investigations in France and the UK have left police no closer to understanding who carried out the al-Hilli murders and why.  Over the years a series of leads have been pursued then dropped.A British national of Iraqi birth, Saad al-Hilli was holidaying with his family in the picturesque countryside of Lake Annecy in eastern France.On the afternoon of 5 September, his body with those of his wife and mother-in-law were found in their car, its motor still running, on a forest road near the village of Chevaline. A passing cyclist had – like the other victims – been shot through the head.Poignantly, the two al-Hilli daughters, aged four and seven, survived. The older girl had been hit on the head with a pistol butt and was badly hurt. The younger, lying in the car under her mother's skirts, was not discovered till forensic experts began examining the scene many hours later.It was fragments from the pistol butt which enabled police to identify it as a Luger P06. The model is regarded more as a collector's item than a working weapon, which made the theory of a professional hit against the family seem less likely.Lake Annecy is only 50km from Switzerland, where the Luger P06 will have been familiar to older people from their military service. French police said many examples of the gun have been kept by families on either side of the border.Among the theories that have been entertained are that the murders were linked to a family row over money; that they were the work of a motiveless crank; and that the main target was the cyclist.Police were also briefly intrigued by the fact that al-Hilli's wife's first husband – an American – died of a heart attack just hours before the killings in France.

schema.headline: Alps murders: Luger in a lake gives hope for French cold case

title: Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West
description: Russian President Vladimir Putin responded with one short sentence when asked at a press conference whether Moscow might strike military facilities in
body: Russian President Vladimir Putin responded with one short sentence when asked at a press conference whether Moscow might strike military facilities in the UK in response to British arms supplies to Ukraine."That's a secret. A military secret."Military secret is not a "yes". And not a "no". It leaves us hanging.And that, I suspect, is the point.Those two words feel like psychological pressure from the Kremlin: to keep Britain guessing - and stressing - over Moscow's intentions, as well as to encourage the UK to think twice about its staunch support for Ukraine.It reminds me of a newspaper article I read a few days ago. Moskovsky Komsomolets had suggested that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham should be seeing Russia, not in his dreams, "but in his nightmares".Scary language. But short on detail about what those nightmares will look like.We cannot conclude that Russian missiles are about to be used against targets in the UK.But look what's happening elsewhere in Europe. Germany now says Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig airport. Putin accused Germany of "planting the evidence". But German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described "the well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe".Could such "operations" now be stepped up in the UK?Yet it wasn't just Britain that received veiled threats at Putin's press conference.So did the West in general. Putin referred to Western countries as sharks."If anyone tries to drag us down the food chain, to gobble us up or devour us, they might get punched in the teeth," he said. "Russia is ready to do that, despite the rapidly growing appetites and teeth of these sharks."Increasingly Russia's president is mixing the geopolitical with the zoological. He recently spoke about killer whales "tearing polar bears apart" to justify Russia's war on Ukraine.The press conference in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, was a fascinating window on Putin's state of mind.For forty-five minutes he took questions from Russian journalists and came across as combative, confident of victory and energised. These days Putin appears most animated when talking about the geopolitical standoff between Russia and the West and the war in Ukraine. Even though the war has not gone to plan. Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield and the country's economy is under considerable pressure."I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble," he declared. Yet the war has lasted more than four-and-a-half years and Ukraine fights on.Officially the Kremlin still calls this a "special military operation". But even Putin now is using the word "war"."War is a brutal and unpredictable thing," he said at the press conference.He claimed that he remained open to negotiations to end the conflict and left no doubt with whom he'd prefer to sit down with from the US administration: Donald Trump's envoys."We are absolutely comfortable working with those people we know well and generally trust," Putin said. "[Jared] Kushner and [Steve] Witkoff are always welcome guests. It's a pleasure working with them."There was no such name check for the CIA director who had made a surprise visit to Moscow last week. The Kremlin says the Russian president didn't meet John Ratcliffe during that trip.Is Putin likely to meet Witkoff and Kushner anytime soon?There's nothing in the diary. Not yet.But if they do head to Moscow, President Trump's envoys will encounter a Kremlin leader who remains determined that any peace in Ukraine should be on Russia's terms.

schema.headline: Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West

title: Tiger Woods gets five-year driving ban after reckless driving plea
description: "I'm completely confident and comfortable with the resolution of this case," Florida  State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl said at a press conference after
body: "I'm completely confident and comfortable with the resolution of this case," Florida  State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl said at a press conference after the hearing.He said he strove to treat Woods like any other defendant."Today I resolved case involving a man who drives a golf ball for a living," Bakkedahl said. "Tomorrow, I'll resolve a case in the same matter for a man who drives a nail for a living."No one was injured in the crash, though Woods had to crawl out through the passenger door to free himself.Police released body camera footage in April that captured the aftermath of the incident, showing the golfing legend after his vehicle clipped a truck and rolled over.In the video, Woods appears calm, kneeling on one knee as he tells officers: "I looked down at my phone, and all of a sudden, boom". He passed a breathalyser test but declined to take a urinalysis screening for other drugs, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said at the time.Woods told officers he had not consumed alcohol that day. When asked about any prescription medication, he responded, "I take a few", adding he had done so earlier that morning. He then listed the medication, though that portion of the footage was redacted.Officers told Woods they suspected his "normal faculties" were impaired by an "unknown substance".Authorities later reported finding two white pills in his pocket, identified as hydrocodone, an opioid commonly prescribed to treat pain.Woods wrote on social media following the incident, "I know and understand the seriousness of the situation I find myself in today."I am stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health. This is necessary in order for me to prioritise my wellbeing and work toward lasting recovery."The incident marked Woods' second arrest on suspicion of driving under the influence.

schema.headline: Tiger Woods gets five-year driving ban after reckless driving plea

title: Madagascar ex-Senate chief Richard Ravalomanana jailed over deadly Gen Z protest crackdown
description: The protests began a year ago, initially sparked by anger over persistent power and water shortages, before developing into a broader movement against
body: The protests began a year ago, initially sparked by anger over persistent power and water shortages, before developing into a broader movement against Rajoelina's government.At least 22 people were killed and more than 100 injured during the unrest, according to UN figures cited by local media.The protests eventually triggered a political crisis that led to Rajoelina's removal from power and the installation of a new administration led by Col Michael Randrianirina.The crackdown was led by the gendarmerie, where Ravalomanana retained considerable influence at the time.He "directed violent actions to suppress the demonstrations", a state prosecutor said in December 2025.Ravalomanana was removed as Senate president in October, shortly after the protests, and was arrested at his home in December after failing to respond to a summons from the gendarmerie.He was later placed in pre-trial detention at the high-security Imerintsiatosika prison outside Antananarivo, where he has spent the past seven months.He is among several senior figures associated with Rajoelina's former government who have faced legal proceedings since the change of power. Ravalomanana is also facing a separate corruption investigation.A former national police chief who testified at the trial backed his account, saying Ravalomanana was not part of the operational chain of command and had issued no orders to police, gendarmes or soldiers deployed during the unrest.His lawyer questioned the evidence linking him directly to the violence."Is there confirmed written or verbal evidence... to accuse him?" he asked the court, arguing that prosecutors had failed to produce proof that security officers had received orders from his client.Ravalomanana's defence team said it would challenge the verdict in a higher court. The court dropped a separate allegation of making a death threat after ruling that the case was too old to prosecute.Known for wearing a cowboy hat and displaying his military medals, Ravalomanana was viewed by protesters as a symbol of authoritarian power.

schema.headline: Madagascar ex-Senate chief Richard Ravalomanana jailed over deadly Gen Z protest crackdown

title: EU and Nato vow to step up pressure on Russia after 'new escalation' in Leipzig
description: The heads of Nato and the European Commission have warned that Russia is growing increasingly reckless and vowed to respond to a "new normal"."Leipzig
body: The heads of Nato and the European Commission have warned that Russia is growing increasingly reckless and vowed to respond to a "new normal"."Leipzig marks a new escalation on European Union soil directly attributed to Russia," said Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a day after Germany blamed Russia for a failed drone attack last month on Leipzig airport."We have to step up and that means being ready to respond to Russia's recklessness faster and better," von der Leyen said. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said the whole alliance, which includes the US, stood "in full solidarity with Germany".Russia has rejected German accusations that a drone carrying explosives deliberately targeted a Ukrainian cargo plane on 4 August.The drone was defused by a robot at Leipzig/Halle airport and a second drone is thought to have collided with another cargo plane.A third drone was reportedly found 10 days later at the airport, which is an important Nato hub and is regularly used by Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft.It was not until Tuesday that the German government said police investigations and intelligence finding had proved that Russia was behind the incidents. The interior minister said that the drone's configuration, components, explosives and detonator were all known from other Russian hybrid operations.Two suspects have reportedly been identified in the Leipzig attack, including a Belarusian with a Russian passport who entered on a tourist visa, and another with Latvian and Russian passports who arrived by plane in Berlin and flew out two days before the failed attack.Von der Leyen was clear in her statement that the Leipzig attack had involved "military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil"."We will not tolerate it," she said.While she was meeting Rutte in Brussels, EU foreign ministers had gathered at Wicklow in Ireland, where France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said action could be taken on a European level against Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" of ships carrying oil and other cargo aimed at avoiding EU sanctions.Barrot and fellow ministers from Belgium and the Netherlands said they had summoned Russian ambassadors in protest at the attack.Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said it was obvious that Russia saw no political cost in its hybrid operations against European allies.The Leipzig attack was part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous incidents, including drones and interference with critical infrastructure, von der Leyen said.Mark Rutte added there had been increased risk to Europeans from drones and missiles crossing into countries on the Alliance's eastern flank, and there had been more "malign activities targeting our territory directly, whether it is fires set in factories producing defence equipment for Ukraine or indeed the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig".Several acts of suspected sabotage have been reported in Germany in the past 24 hours alone, including two attacks on electricity substations, one in the east and one in the west near Cologne.Although authorities do not yet know who was behind the incidents, North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said an attack that targeted power lines at Bergheim in western Germany was deliberate and whoever had carried out was attacking the country as a whole."We are investigating two possibilities: sabotage directed by a foreign state and left-wing extremism," he said.Several power lines failed prompting five power plant units to go offline at two separate coal-fired power stations. Police said six launching devices had been found in a field.High-voltage power lines were damaged near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant in Brandenburg early on Tuesday and explosive devices were later found at a substation.Meanwhile, in neighbouring Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a fire at a factory producing combat drones at Skarżysko-Kamienna, 140km (85 miles) south of Warsaw was a deliberate act of arson and sabotage. Arson has also not been ruled out in a fire at a factory in Lublin on Sunday night.Von der Leyen said sanctions had already been used to deter Russia, and EU foreign ministers were discussing further ways of "cutting deeper in Russia's war chest".The EU has already agreed to loan Ukraine €90bn (£77bn), and von der Leyen said Kyiv had asked for billions of extra euros in funding to help pay for PAC-3 air defence missiles. Work was already taking place on a joint Europe-Ukraine Freyja anti-ballistic missile defence project, she added.She promised that Europe and Nato would just maintain pressure on Moscow but "we will increase it and we will not stop, not until Russia stops bombing and killing innocent children, men and children in Ukraine".

schema.headline: EU and Nato vow to step up pressure on Russia after 'new escalation' in Leipzig

title: Autonomous aircraft: Pilot-free crop dusters lead the way
description: Over an alfalfa field in California's San Joaquin Valley, a small crop-spraying plane is flying scarily low to the ground. There's little risk to huma
body: Over an alfalfa field in California's San Joaquin Valley, a small crop-spraying plane is flying scarily low to the ground. There's little risk to humans though, as the plane is pilot-free."We can actually go lower than a human pilot can," says Russ Marotzke, as the aircraft skims over the crop.Flying lower means less spray drift and therefore less chemicals are needed than in conventional manned crop-dusting, he says.The pilotless plane belongs to Pyka, where Marotzke works as a flight test engineer.Based in a converted Second World War hangar overlooking San Francisco Bay, the start-up makes self-flying aircraft without cockpits, designed either to spray crops or deliver cargo.It is among a small group of companies racing to bring autonomous fixed-wing aircraft into commercial service.Flying urban air taxis, so called electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, have captured much of the attention around autonomous aviation.But a quieter race is also under way to deploy self-flying planes, first for jobs like crop spraying and cargo delivery – and eventually, many of their makers hope, carrying passengers too."A fully scaled, ubiquitous passenger operation is the holy grail," says Michael Norcia, Pyka's co-founder and CEO, who envisions a large fleet of minibus-capacity Pyka planes ferrying passengers up and down the US east and west coasts."There's a decent chance we'll get to that point before the eVTOL industry."I've come to one of Pyka's crop-sprayer test sites, about 80km (50 miles) east of the company's factory and reached by a bumpy dirt road.Today, Marotzke and a colleague are trying out a software update on a demonstration aircraft.About a dozen Pyka aircraft are already in Brazil where they are used to spray crops such as cotton and soybeans, work previously carried out by human pilots.The crop-spraying plane is fully electric, with its battery in the nose. It can fly for about 35 minutes and carries up to 300L of spray in a tank in its middle.Pyka's planes are sometimes called large drones, but it seems an understatement: they all have 11.5m wingspans.Inside a shipping container beside the field, the engineers highlight on a computer the area they want the aircraft to spray. The software then plans the route, taking account of obstacles such as nearby power lines that have already been mapped.The take-off, down a runway beside the field, is seamless. About 15 minutes later, after sensing that it is running low on spray – water for today's purposes – the aircraft lands itself for a manual refill and demonstration battery swap. It then takes to the air again to resume spraying precisely where it left off.Autonomous flight is different from autopilot.Autopilot assists, much like cruise control and lane-keeping functions in a car.Autonomous systems aim to handle the entire flight, including take-off and landing, with little or no human intervention, using algorithms to process sensor data and control the aircraft.Self-flying planes have been slower to emerge than self-driving cars, despite operating in what is generally considered a more structured and predictable environment.That is partly because big tech companies "doubled down" on cars, pouring vast sums into the technology, says Mykel Kochenderfer, an expert in safe aviation autonomy at Stanford University.But it is also because aircraft are held to stricter safety standards than cars, creating a much higher bar for deployment."The consequences for air accidents can just be so severe," says Kochenderfer.Military interest has been helping propel the technology. Many of the companies have defence contracts to demonstrate and trial their systems, often with fewer regulatory hurdles than on the civilian side, and some are even already supplying military customers, external.In the US, the largest autonomous fixed-wing aircraft approved for commercial civilian use so far is Pyka's crop sprayer, which won authorization last year.Though operations are limited to a tightly defined agricultural setting and require a ground operator and visual observer. It earlier secured similar approval in Brazil, where rules are more permissive.Pyka aims to scale up production from around two dozen planes a year currently to 1000 by 2030. Each sells for $550,000, with customers trained to operate them.The UK has yet to approve any such longer-term operations, though British firm Windracers is seeking permission to launch an autonomous cargo service in Shetland and Orkney. Its aircraft, designed to carry goods to remote areas, are also flying missions in Ukraine."It would be the first heavy-lift air cargo service by drone certainly in the UK and probably anywhere," says Stephen Wright, Windracers founder and chairman.Supporters say autonomous aircraft could address pilot shortages, remove people from dangerous work such as crop spraying, improve efficiency – for example, by  allowing aircraft to carry more cargo – and cut costs if one operator can oversee many planes.They also argue automation could make flying safer, pointing to past declines in accidents as more automated systems have been introduced.Pilots' groups remain wary.The US Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA) calls removing pilots "a serious gamble with safety and a step too far".The US National Agricultural Aviation Association, which represents crop dusting pilots, says small uncrewed aircraft can be hard for its aviators to see. Piloted planes, it adds, can spray a much larger area faster.Pyka and Windracers are building aircraft from scratch, arguing this allows autonomy to be designed in from the outset and the aircraft tailored to the job.Others are retrofitting existing larger planes.Backed by Boeing's investment arm, US-based Reliable Robotics is currently testing its system on the Cessna 208B Grand Caravan, a single-pilot cargo plane that can carry about 1360kg of payload over hundreds of kilometers.Retrofitting on certified aircraft lets the company focus exclusively on proving the autonomous system's safety rather than also having to seek approval for a new aircraft, says Robert Rose, its co-founder and CEO.Merlin Labs, also US-based, has been working its way up through progressively larger military aircraft and is now applying its system to the two-pilot Lockheed Martin C-130J military transport plane, with commercial multi-crew cargo planes next."It is a common autonomy brain that can transition between different aircraft," explains Matt George, Merlin's founder and CEO.The companies also differ in their approach to AI.Reliable is avoiding it altogether, arguing it would complicate certification.Merlin, meanwhile, is taking a far more AI-centric approach.The divide is evident in so-called detect and avoid systems.One of autonomous flight's biggest challenges is replicating a pilot's ability to spot and maneuver safely around other aircraft and obstacles, and there is virtually no margin for error.With no perfect solution yet, companies are adding different sensor systems as well as duplicating those that already come as standard to provide extra back-up.Reliable has added forward-looking air-to-air radar to detect other aircraft more than eight kilometers ahead, with software that follows fixed rules to decide how the plane should respond.It is "better than a pilot's eyeballs" says Rose.Merlin, meanwhile, is using AI-powered cameras to detect and classify objects.Pyka has used lidar from the outset to detect trees, vehicles, large birds and terrain. But it's short range, so the company also plans to add AI-powered cameras, its first real use of AI onboard."For a lot of things there's no need to use AI…but for figuring out that six pixels in the distance are an airplane versus some other smudge, it is perfect territory," says Norcia.The AI dilemma also extends to communicating with air traffic control.In shared airspace, aircraft must be able to receive, interpret and respond to radio instructions, typically from air traffic control.Reliable's solution is to have a remote pilot on the ground, initially fully trained, to handle communications and make safety-critical decisions.Merlin plans to use generative AI, trained on thousands of hours of recorded exchanges, to interpret instructions and respond itself."Our problem is harder… but we want to move beyond remote piloting," says George.Merlin plans to reduce pilots in stages, from two to one and eventually none.Pyka, says Norcia, is content to let others "blaze the trail" in finding the best way to operate in shared airspace.Meanwhile, even if fully autonomous passenger flight remains elusive, many expect the technology being pioneered will inch into commercial aviation, potentially making piloted flying safer.That, notes ALPA, the US pilots' association, would be a welcome development.

schema.headline: Autonomous aircraft: Pilot-free crop dusters lead the way

title: Charlie Kirk murder suspect Tyler Robinson pleads not guilty as judge clears way for death penalty trial
description: The defendant, wearing a grey suit and occasionally consulting with his lawyers, appeared in court in the city of Provo on Tuesday.Kirk's widow, Erika
body: The defendant, wearing a grey suit and occasionally consulting with his lawyers, appeared in court in the city of Provo on Tuesday.Kirk's widow, Erika, the mother of their two children, and his parents, ⁠Robert and Kathryn, were also at the hearing.In a statement shared afterwards, the Kirk family said the judge's decision "marks an important step" in their "pursuit of justice". "Every step in this process carries the weight of all that Charlie's murder has taken from his family, especially his children who will grow up without their father," the statement added.Closing arguments followed a five-day preliminary hearing in July, during which prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial. That included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs."There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court on Tuesday, outlining video that he said showed Robinson "dressed to kill" on campus on the day of the shooting."We know that the defendant is the shooter… first, because of the video evidence; second, because of the DNA; third, because of his admissions; and fourth, because of circumstantial evidence," McBride said.Prosecutors said the accused, a former apprentice electrician, was in a relationship with his roommate and regarded Kirk's conservative views, particularly on transgender issues, as "repugnant" - which they argued was the motive.On Tuesday, prosecutors also outlined "aggravating" factors - accusing the defendant of "gambling with the lives of others" when he allegedly fired towards Kirk, who was surrounded by other people."He was playing, in effect, a game of ballistic roulette," prosecutor Chad Grunander said."It's been 356 days since Tyler Robinson assassinated Charlie Kirk," Grunander added. "It's time for him, the defendant, to be bound over for trial and arraigned. Today."Defence lawyers attempted to sow doubt about the prosecution's evidence. During July's hearing, they raised questions about procedure and the credentials of experts who testified. Robinson's lawyers have repeatedly objected to cameras livestreaming court proceedings.Judge Tony Graf again listened to arguments on the issue during a sealed hearing on Tuesday morning before closing arguments began - but he ruled in favour of transparency in a case that has sparked conspiracy theories.On Tuesday, the defence sought to downplay the aggravating factors outlined by prosecutors - arguing that no bullets hit anyone in the crowd apart from Kirk.The court heard and saw during July's hearing how the accused allegedly scouted the campus repeatedly on the day Kirk was shot - interacting with TPUSA members and eating Chick-fil-A before returning in different clothes.The new outfit included "long pants to obscure the rifle he had concealed down his pants", McBride said on Tuesday.According to prosecutors' evidence presented during the July hearing, Robinson's DNA was found on his grandfather's rifle stashed in a wooden area near campus after the shooting, as well as on a towel it was wrapped in and a screwdriver recovered at the scene.McBride also told the court on Tuesday that engravings found on casings from the shooting allegedly matched a Dremel tool recovered at the home the defendant shared with his roommate.Twiggs' videotaped interview with prosecutors was played in July during the hearing. Robinson's roommate testified that the defendant had confessed to the shooting, cried and said he wished he hadn't done it.Robinson, in the company of his family and a neighbour, turned himself in the day after the murder.He is next due in court on 23 October, when a trial date is expected to be set.

schema.headline: Charlie Kirk murder suspect Tyler Robinson pleads not guilty as judge clears way for death penalty trial

title: USS Abraham Lincoln: US sailors arrive in Thailand's Pattaya after record 250 days at sea
description: Figure caption, Watch: Why US troops have a history in this raucous Thai cityByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondentReporting fromPattaya, Thaila
body: Figure caption, Watch: Why US troops have a history in this raucous Thai cityByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondentReporting fromPattaya, ThailandUpdated 5 hours agoAfter a record 250 days at sea without a port stop, the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has docked in Thailand, giving its nearly 5,000 crew members a much-needed break.The ship is docking close to the beach resort of Pattaya, known for its raucous nightlife and for sex tourism. For the US it also carries strong historical echoes.When the weary sailors walk into the city's bars and restaurants, they will be treading in the footsteps of the hundreds of thousands of US troops who came here for R&R – rest and relaxation - during the Vietnam War.They transformed it from a sleepy fishing village to one of the world's most famous and frenetic party towns.Today the neon-lit alleys running down to the beach are much quieter than usual. The bars in the city's famous Walking Street still screen videos on their walls of pole-dancing women, trying to lure customers inside.But there are not many of those customers, and most seem to be family groups from the Middle East more interested in the Turkish ice-cream vendor than the go-go bars.The Iran War, which has affected tourism and consumer spending, has hit businesses hard here. The prospect of thousands of American sailors, with nine months of salary unspent while at sea, offers a rare opportunity to local businesses.Image source, ReutersImage caption, US personnel arriving at the Hard Rock Hotel in Pattaya on WednesdayThe US carrier left San Diego last November on what was supposed to be a six-month assignment in the Pacific and South China Sea. However, the ship was diverted to the Gulf after the US and Israel began military operations against Iran in late February.Recently some members of Congress raised concern about reports of food shortages, broken toilets and mental stress among the crew. The US Navy acknowledged that working conditions have been tough, but said the crew were sufficiently well-supported. It would not, however, comment to the BBC on the carrier docking at Pattaya, citing operational security.Despite its close relationship with China, Thailand is a treaty ally of the US, and port visits by US Navy ships are a familiar occurrence.But this is probably the largest number of US military personnel coming straight from a war zone to Pattaya since the fall of Saigon in 1975.Image source, BBC/Lulu LuoImage caption, Pattaya's streets, know for their raucous nightlife, are quieter than usual"This visit could be our best hope," said Anon Saiteer, who sells gems in a shop near Walking Street, which has put up a large sign welcoming the US sailors and marines and offering them a special discount. "We have nothing to lose – we just hope they will spend some money here."But US and Thai officials are trying to ensure this happens without any of the salacious headlines for which Pattaya has become known.The Thai authorities have said there are a few places where the US servicemen and women will not be allowed to go. One of them is Soi 6, which runs down to the main beach, and is known for its concentration of racy go-go bars.While the Thai police have reminded their US visitors that prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand, there are actually thought to be 25,000 to 50,000 sex workers in the city. Many of them work in Soi 6, where they stand outside the bars imploring men to come inside.The many cannabis shops in Pattaya are also off-limits to US crew members, along with sea-sports like paragliding and jet-skis."It is their decision," Mayor Poramase Ngampiches told the BBC.  "The US military have done their homework."Image source, BBC/Lulu LuoImage caption, The war in Iran is hurting local businesses US Naval Attache Kristopher Robinson rebuffed questions from the BBC about activities that soldiers were banned from doing.Instead, he said the US troops would "conduct themselves in accordance with US law, US naval regulations, and the laws of Thailand"."We're trying to give the sailors as much opportunity for rest as they can," he said.The US Navy has organised shuttle buses from the port into Pattaya running from 5am to 2am every day the carrier is here in Thailand. Two hotels have been designated suitable for those US crew members who want to splash out on a night onshore.The Thai authorities have deployed hundreds of police officers to keep an eye on the city's entertainment zones, and warned local businesses not to overcharge their American guests."The visits of US military men 50-60 years ago introduced Pattaya to the world and turned it into a tourist attraction," says Mayor Poramase. "We have to be frank, the city has a reputation for bar girls. We understand the stereotypes. We can't stop that. "What we can do is to show that Pattaya has changed, that we now have other things, such as sports, seminars, wellness and family-friendly activities. It's a mixture of everything."Both countries hope that by the time the USS Abraham Lincoln begins the long journey home across the Pacific on 6 September, it will be with a refreshed and rested crew.With additional reporting from Nongnapat Patcham.

schema.headline: USS Abraham Lincoln: US sailors arrive in Thailand's Pattaya after record 250 days at sea

title: BBC travels inside occupied Lebanon as officials say Israel is expanding positions
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC sees Israeli military presence in southern LebanonByMiddle East correspondentReporting fromsouthern LebanonThe drive on the
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC sees Israeli military presence in southern LebanonByMiddle East correspondentReporting fromsouthern LebanonThe drive on the highway by the Mediterranean in southern Lebanon, near the border with Israel, is scenic and, these days, desolate. Crops lie abandoned and buildings destroyed by Israeli air strikes, too many to count, are in ruins.Near the town of Naqoura, a Lebanese military checkpoint, painted in the white-and-red colours of the national flag, is the last visible sign of the state's presence. Soldiers are positioned behind concrete walls, but the road is empty. A few minutes further south, around a dozen Israeli flags indicate the start of occupied territory. Unless authorised by Israel, no-one can enter.This part of the country is the heartland of Lebanon's Shia Muslim community, from which Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed militia and political party, gets most of its support. It has seen three invasions by the Israeli military in wars against the group in the last two decades alone. The most recent started in March, after Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel following the killing of the Iranian supreme leader, at the start of the US and Israel's war against Iran.Last month, a BBC team joined a humanitarian mission of the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon, known as Unifil, which is one of the only ways to visit the area under Israeli control. There, as it did in Gaza, Israel has flattened entire villages, and air strikes and demolitions have continued even after a ceasefire was announced in June.Image source, Neha Sharma/BBCImage caption, An Israeli soldier at a checkpoint established in a residential building near the Unifil headquarters in NaqouraLed by Finnish troops who are part of Unifil, the convoy was escorting civilians to and from Christian villages near the border. Those communities were spared from Israel's attacks and invasion during the war and, with the surrounding areas now under occupation, are now cut off from the rest of the country. Our presence was allowed by the Israeli military through a deconfliction mechanism with the UN.The strip of land currently controlled by Israel constitutes around 5% of Lebanese territory and, in some places, extends 10km (six miles) from the border. Driving along the wall that separates the two countries, we saw service roads built by Israel after the invasion, intense movement of Israeli soldiers and residential buildings that were being used by them. Some were covered in netting to protect them from Hezbollah's explosive drones.We also heard Israeli surveillance drones in the sky and explosions in the distance, possibly from demolitions being carried out by Israel in villages that are under occupation.Image source, Neha Sharma/BBCImage caption, Israeli soldiers drive on a road along the wall separating Lebanon and IsraelIn a visit to occupied southern Lebanon last month, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said he had instructed the military to "take all necessary steps to prepare for a long-term presence in the area". Israeli officials say their goal is to establish what they call a "security zone" to protect communities in northern Israel from rockets and drones that have been fired by Hezbollah from southern Lebanon, as well as a possible ground invasion.According to Unifil, the Israeli military has established four new bases in the invaded areas, bringing the number of such positions to nine. Israeli forces had remained in five points after invading southern Lebanon during the previous war against Hezbollah in 2024, in violation of the deal that ended that conflict."In the past months, we've seen the consolidation and fortification of Israeli positions, construction of protective infrastructure, and other engineering works," Kandice Ardiel, a Unifil spokeswoman, said. "We have [also] observed what appear to be Israeli civilian personnel carrying out demolition and engineering activities in support of military activities in south Lebanon."Human rights groups say some of Israel's actions in southern Lebanon amount to the deliberate destruction of civilian infrastructure, a possible war crime. Hundreds of thousands of Lebanese remain displaced, without knowing when, or if, they will be able to return.In response to our questions, the Israeli military said the buildings that had been destroyed were used by Hezbollah for military purposes, and that it operated in accordance with international law. It did not respond to other specific questions about its actions in the occupied areas.Image source, Neha Sharma/BBCImage caption, Some of the houses used by the Israeli military are covered in netting to protect them from Hezbollah's explosive dronesIn June, the US and Iran announced a preliminary deal aimed at ending their conflict, which included a cessation of the violence in Lebanon. Since then, a Lebanese intelligence official told me, Lebanon's military has recorded more than 5,000 violations of the deal by Israel, including air strikes, drone attacks, shelling and near-daily incursions of Israeli soldiers into Lebanese territory beyond the area under occupation, the so-called Yellow Line.As it does in Gaza, the Israeli military justifies some of its attacks in Lebanon as operations against what it describes as immediate threats. In many cases, however, it is not clear how immediate these alleged threats are or if there is any threat at all. Hezbollah, which is considered a terrorist organisation by countries including the UK and the US, has not carried out attacks against Israel since the ceasefire came into force, but has targeted Israeli troops operating inside Lebanese territory."[The Israelis] are expanding their presence [in Lebanon]. They've [also] been setting areas ablaze, demolishing houses while the bombing continues, despite the ceasefire," the Lebanese intelligence official said. "It's clear that they don't want anyone to go back [to those villages] in the coming year, or even years. This isn't only about Hezbollah. This is about preventing people from returning."Image source, Neha Sharma/BBCImage caption, Entire villages along the border have been destroyed by IsraelIsraeli officials have conditioned a withdrawal from Lebanon on Hezbollah's disarmament, something the Lebanese government cannot deliver without the group's consent. Hezbollah, observers say, is still a significant military force despite the setbacks in the recent wars. Both countries have held direct talks that resulted in a framework agreement brokered by the US: Israel would pull out of certain areas, called "pilot zones", where Lebanese army soldiers would be deployed and Hezbollah's disarmament would be verified.Hezbollah opposes the efforts – the group's leader, Naim Qassem, called them "surrender with humiliation" last week – and says any discussion about its weapons should only happen after a full Israeli withdrawal. Israel, for its part, has claimed that the Lebanese national military, which rejects the use of force against the group saying this could pit Lebanese against Lebanese, has not done enough.The plan has seen no progress, and there is no expectation of any significant change before the Israeli election at the end of October."The idea of the 'pilot zones' seems to be dead until the context changes," a European diplomat familiar with the situation told me. "It seems we're heading to a Gaza-like situation. The Israelis are entrenching themselves... and are here to stay, for now."

schema.headline: BBC travels inside occupied Lebanon as officials say Israel is expanding positions

title: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of peopleByLyse DoucetChief international correspondentReporting
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of peopleByLyse DoucetChief international correspondentReporting fromTorkham crossing and KabulThe elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind."It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins."But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.The expulsions show no sign of stopping. Image source, AFPImage caption, Trucks carrying returnees parked along the highway near the border The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR."In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan."We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all."I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry."We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says. "But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Afghan returnees deported from Pakistan arriving at the Torkham crossing Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law". Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".Image caption, Zarina, 40, is among the million Afghan who have returned this year alone Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children. Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified."I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house. "We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work."I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country. Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.  But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.Image caption, Zarina says she is worried about the future of the girls who cannot attend secondary school and university in Taliban-run AfghanistanAt the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face."There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide. The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition."No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girls' education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states. As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"He answers his own question: "Nothing."We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense. All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

schema.headline: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban

title: South Korea: Disabled care home head jailed for sexually assaulting residents
description: A South Korean court has jailed the former head of a disabled care home for sexually assaulting multiple residents, in a case that shocked the nation.
body: A South Korean court has jailed the former head of a disabled care home for sexually assaulting multiple residents, in a case that shocked the nation.The man, surnamed Kim, was handed a 15-year prison term for abusing three residents at the Saekdongwon facility in Incheon City, west of Seoul. The ruling is subject to appeal.Police started investigating Kim after one of his victims, a woman with a severe intellectual disability, came forward in February last year.The case has prompted the government to inspect 1,507 care facilities for disabled people across the country, where 33 cases of suspected abuse were found.South Korean Prime Minister Kim Min-seok had described the abuse at Saekdongwon as "a grave matter that calls into question the very reason for the state's existence".An in-depth assessment of residents commissioned by Ganghwa County found that 20 current and former female residents may have experienced sexual abuse.Many in South Korea have asked how such a case could still occur, especially after laws were strengthened in 2011 to protect people with disabilities from sexual assault.Some have also raised questions on how the director's actions could have gone undetected for so long.Ganghwa County has ordered Saekdongwon to close, while Incheon City officials revoked the licence of the foundation that operated it.However, the closure has been deferred until the remaining residents have been relocated and arrangements for independent living have been completed.The foundation has filed an administrative lawsuit challenging the revocation of its licence.

schema.headline: South Korea: Disabled care home head jailed for sexually assaulting residents

title: Remarkable US oil deal puzzles analysts - and angers many Venezuelans
description: From the moment elite US troops swooped into Nicolás Maduro's compound in Caracas to forcibly remove him from power in January, President Donald Trump
body: From the moment elite US troops swooped into Nicolás Maduro's compound in Caracas to forcibly remove him from power in January, President Donald Trump made clear that securing control over Venezuela's oil resources was a key goal of his administration.The United States would "run" Venezuela, he said at the time, and manage the sale of Venezuelan oil for the foreseeable future.The signing of a huge US-Venezuela oil deal in Caracas on Wednesday marks the fruition of that plan. The agreement grants a US-led company 100-year concessions over 17 oilfields in Venezuela, amounting to a staggering 65 billion barrels of crude. That equates to more than a fifth of the country's proven oil reserves.Beyond the eye-watering numbers, both sides heralded the deal as good for their respective nations. President Trump called it "the biggest oil deal in world history", while the interim Venezuelan President, Delcy Rodríguez, said the agreement was "historic", and would generate $100bn (£74bn) in investment and more than $200bn in tax revenue.Others profoundly disagreed."This is a terrible deal. [Rodríguez] has given away 20% of the national patrimony for nothing," said Trump's former special representative on Venezuela and Iran, Elliott Abrams. "I think she is simply complying with the demands she's getting from Washington."On Tuesday, the White House released a fact sheet which set out some details of the deal's framework. The US government will work alongside a private business in Venezuela called North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep), the second largest private oil producer in Venezuela after Chevron.One extraordinary detail of how the Trump administration will work with Nabep is that the US government will have "veto power over the appointment of any member of the board of directors, and a majority of Nabep's board of directors must be US citizens".With the ongoing US war with Iran increasing prices at the petrol pumps, a boost in oil production outside of the Middle East could affect consumers. Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum told Fox Business the pact was "shifting the geopolitical centre of the global energy markets" away from what he called the "choke points in the Middle East" and back to the Western Hemisphere.There is a logic to the US-Venezuela partnership, Elliott Abrams argued, while Gulf oil supplies are currently so unreliable. But he said the terms are so one-sided they are a "kind of fever dream of what colonialism looks like".The White House has spoken of the deal having "re-established the Monroe Doctrine", an 19th Century principle exerting US power across South America - "purging foreign malign influence from our backyard and ensuring American dominance in our hemisphere is never again questioned".Despite the insistence from both governments that the plan will benefit both Venezuelans and Americans, it is not without pitfalls and clear unanswered questions.The proposed timeframe alone is problematic. Trump has said the agreement will generate profit within two or three years. Energy experts, however, warn the dire state of the Venezuelan oil sector means a decade is more realistic.Luis Pacheco, of the Baker Institute at Rice University in Houston, told BBC Mundo that Venezuela needs to invest about $100bn over eight years in order to return to its oil production levels of 30 years ago."It's important to know who will manage those resources and for what purpose," Pacheco said. "Are they going to put the same people in charge of managing that money who already squandered the biggest oil boom of the century?" he asked, referring to past mismanagement of the country's oil wealth.The Venezuelan opposition is concerned the deal deepens President Trump's relationship with Delcy Rodríguez, whom they accuse of heading the same regime as Maduro. The Trump administration not only decried Maduro's government as a corrupt drug cartel, but surrounded Venezuela with the biggest armada of the modern era.The ease and speed with which Washington has now pivoted to working with Maduro's former vice-president infuriates the opposition.The Nobel Peace Prize winner and presidential hopeful, María Corina Machado, may choose not to publicly criticise President Trump, whose support she needs if she hopes to come to power. Others, though, have been more forthcoming."You chose to use the power of the United States not to liberate Venezuelans, but to ally yourself with our oppressors," said Venezuelan economist, Ricardo Hausmann, on social media, directing his comments at the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio."You opted to push through an asset seizure, an unconstitutional agreement with an illegitimate and oppressive government, instead of using the leadership of the United States to first restore constitutional order and democracy," he said.The lack of an imminent election in Venezuela – or, indeed, any clear plan towards one – strikes many opponents as a betrayal.There is betrayal felt at the other end of the ideological spectrum, too. Although the governing socialist party, PSUV, has backed Rodríguez over the US deal, many Venezuelan socialists see it as capitulation.After almost three decades opposing Washington's influence in the region, they feel she has gifted the country's most valuable asset to the old enemy.The deal "hands over [the oil] and opens the doors to a new colonialism of the United States," said Rafael Ramírez, who served as the head of the state-run energy firm, PDVSA, and as the oil minister under former President Hugo Chávez.In early 2008, Chávez presented his Sunday television programme, Aló Presidente, from former ExxonMobil oilfields in the Orinoco River Belt. Having expropriated some of the oil company's assets in the region, he was in a defiant mood."We have the reins in our hands and we won't ever let them go again," he said of the state-run oil company's ownership of oilfields, and denounced how previous Washington-friendly governments had turned Venezuela into "a nation of gringos"."It was a theft of our nation but the Bolivarian Revolution has put a stop to it," he thundered to applause from PDVSA employees.Yet it was one of his disciples – his handpicked successor's successor – who has now signed this opaque deal with Washington and praised it as a victory for Venezuela.

schema.headline: Remarkable US oil deal puzzles analysts - and angers many Venezuelans

title: Zelensky says airlines should avoid Russian airspace as Ukraine escalates drone operations
description: Ukraine's president has told airlines that Russian airspace will be "effectively closing" as his country escalates its drone strikes. "We want to warn
body: Ukraine's president has told airlines that Russian airspace will be "effectively closing" as his country escalates its drone strikes. "We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, everyone who still uses key Russian airports: the Russian sky is becoming completely dangerous," Volodymyr Zelensky said. Ukraine has since formally notified the UN of the risks to civilian aviation.Russian President Vladimir Putin said the comments amounted to a "declaration of state terrorism". Most Western commercial airlines do not fly over Russia because of the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine, but carriers in countries like Turkey and China do.Explaining the elevated airspace risk in his nightly video address on Tuesday, Zelensky said that "Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such - not a single civilian aircraft" and did not want the loss of innocent lives."There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said.Zelensky directed the warning to airlines continuing to operate flights to Russian airports, especially in major cities like St Petersburg and Moscow.In a statement on X, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that Ukraine had officially notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that Russian airspace was not safe for civilian aviation."We want to prevent unintended incidents," he said, adding: "The war is returning home to Russia."On Wednesday afternoon, flight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed many planes flying over Russia, including arriving and departing from the two main airports.Several airlines that fly through Russia told the BBC that they were carefully monitoring the situation.Qatar Airways, which flies into Moscow and travels through Russian airspace to get to the US west coast, said its flight planning was "guided by rigorous and continuous monitoring of airspace security, safety assessments, and geopolitical developments".FlyDubai, an Emirati government-owned carrier, told the BBC that it would "closely monitor the evolving situation in the region and adjust our flight schedules and routings as necessary".Ukraine has targeted energy facilities deep inside Russian territory and there have been repeated attacks on depots belonging to Russia's two biggest online retailers, Wildberries and Ozon. Its drone attacks have for months led to disruption at some of Russia's biggest airports, especially in Moscow where at times all four major airports have been forced to halt arrivals and departures. Several cancellations were reported on Wednesday.Ukraine does not have to target airports to cause disruption.Under Russia's air defence "Kovyor" (carpet) plan, flights are suspended if a drone is detected in the relevant area. Aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said in an alert to clients that while the majority of Ukraine's drone and missile strikes were likely to occur within 300km (186 miles) of the border, daily attacks deeper inside Russia were almost certain to continue this year."There is also a realistic possibility that the frequency of Ukrainian strikes will continue to increase in the short term deep inside Russian territory," the alert added. "It is assessed that miscalculation and/or misidentification is likely in areas related to the Ukraine conflict."Speaking to reporters at the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin said: "They are asking us to resume negotiations... but you don't negotiate with terrorists."His comments come as Russia's attacks on Ukraine continue, with heavy strikes killing 12 people on Tuesday and further attacks on Odesa, Sumy and Kyiv on Wednesday. Russia's military has said it is preparing to carry out "massive" strikes on Ukrainian power stations.The Ukrainian capital and its surrounding region have come under attack for seven days in a row.A few weeks ago, Zelensky said Russia was attacking Ukraine every day, and Ukraine's military had "begun the process of bringing the war back to Russia". At the weekend he said the same, that Russia had to feel the war was "returning to where it came from".Putin acknowledged that Ukrainian strikes had damaged infrastructure inside Russia, while insisting that "only 10%" of oil refineries were left to repair. Chinese, Turkish and Gulf state airlines are among those using Russian airspace, with savings in time and fuel on routes between Asia and Europe.    Other carriers have largely avoided the eastern European region since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February, 2022.Ukraine has closed its airspace to civilian aircraft throughout that period.The risks of civil aviation during a war are clear. A few months after war broke out in eastern Ukraine in 2014 between Russian-backed separatists and the Ukrainian military, a Russian-made missile brought down a passenger plane, killing all 298 people on board.Last year, the UN aviation agency ruled that Russia was responsible for the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine in July 2014.The Kremlin has always denied any responsibility for the air disaster.In 2024, Putin apologised to the president of neighbouring Azerbaijan over the downing of a commercial airliner in Russian airspace, in which 38 people were killed.He said the "tragic incident" had occurred when Russian air defence systems were repelling Ukrainian drones.

schema.headline: Zelensky says airlines should avoid Russian airspace as Ukraine escalates drone operations

title: Odisha: Why Dara Singh, murderer of Christian missionary Graham Staines and his sons, may walk free in India
description: Warning: This article contains details of violent death that some readers may find distressingOne of India's most shocking incidents of anti-Christian
body: Warning: This article contains details of violent death that some readers may find distressingOne of India's most shocking incidents of anti-Christian violence is back in the news more than a quarter of a century after it drew condemnation from around the world.The Supreme Court is hearing a petition seeking release from prison by a man who is convicted of killing Australian Christian missionary Graham Staines and his two young sons in 1999.Dara Singh - whose real name is Rabindra Kumar Pal - has been in jail since his arrest in 2000, serving a life sentence for burning alive the Australian missionary and his six and 10-year-old sons in a village in the eastern state of Odisha (formerly Orissa).Staines had spent 30 years working with leprosy patients, but Singh and his associates from Hindu hardline groups had accused him of forcibly converting poor Hindus from disadvantaged castes and tribals to Christianity.The viciousness of the crime sent shockwaves through India's minority Christian community and caused global outrage. Now reports that Singh may be set free have brought alive memories of the heinous crime.Staines lived in Baripada in Mayurbhanj district, where he worked among the local tribal community.On the night of their murder on 22 January 1999, Staines and his sons had attended a Christian gathering in Manoharpur, a remote village in the neighbouring district of Keonjhar. They were sleeping in their jeep when a mob of 60 to 70 people led by Singh surrounded their vehicle, set fire to it and prevented them from escaping.As Singh went on the run after the crime, police put up posters all over the state, offering an 800,000-rupee (approximately $18,000 then) reward for information leading to his capture. Reports at the time said he was helped by villagers and tribals who eulogised him as "a modern-day Tarzan who plays with elephants and rides tigers". He was arrested a year later during an overnight raid on a jungle hideout.In a sensational interview, external with the India Today magazine's Ruben Banerjee from prison a few months later, he denied killing Staines and his children but said he "did not like Graham Staines" and had "spearheaded the movement against missionaries". "Missionaries have been targeting our religion. They have been converting Hindus by deceit and inducements. Our religion is under siege. As a true Hindu, it was my responsibility to oppose them," he said. "Since I was possibly the most famous name in the region, the police implicated me in the killings."Singh added that he was "prepared to be a martyr for the cause of Hindus" but believed that he would never get convicted.His optimism was misplaced - in 2003, a trial court sentenced Singh to death and 12 others to life imprisonment. Two years later, the high court commuted his death sentence. It confirmed the life term of his accomplice Mahendra Hembram but freed 11 others, saying there was not enough evidence to support their convictions.In January 2011, the Supreme Court upheld Singh's life sentence, refusing the prosecutors' plea to reinstate the death penalty.The Staines murder was not the only crime Singh was guilty of. In 2007, he was convicted for two other heinous crimes he committed against religious minorities in 1999 - the same year he murdered the Australian missionary and his children.He received life sentences, external for leading a mob that set fire to a church and killed Catholic priest Arul Das with an arrow as he tried to flee the burning building and, in the second instance, for beating and burning to death a Muslim garment trader Shaikh Rahaman.Police had registered 10 cases accusing Singh of involvement in hijacking trucks of Muslim traders transporting cows - an animal many Hindus consider sacred - and setting them free. In his interview, Singh denied being "involved personally", saying "my supporters might have done it". But he admitted that he was "actively involved in the movement against illegal trade in cows and cowslaughter" which "had to be stopped at any cost".Church leaders had alleged the attacks were carried out at the behest of hardline Hindu organisation Bajrang Dal but Singh denied he was a member and an enquiry commission, led by retired top court judge DP Wadhwa, later ruled that he had worked alone.Graham Staines' widow, Gladys, who stayed on in India with her daughter Esther until July 2004, said she had "forgiven" Dara Singh in the Christian spirit. "Forgiveness opens up the path of healing," she said.In July 2024, Singh filed a plea for remission in the top court, saying he was entitled to be released because he had spent more than 25 years in prison. He said his conduct had been good in jail and expressed remorse for his actions.The 62-year-old blamed the crime on "the fervour of youth" in his petition, external seeking early release. "The petitioner acknowledges and deeply regrets the transgressions committed more than two decades ago."In the fervour of youth, fuelled by impassioned reactions to the brutal history of India, the petitioner's psyche momentarily lost restraint and it is imperative for the court to scrutinise not merely the actions but the underlying intent, noting that there was no personal animosity harboured towards any victim," he wrote.Last year, the top court asked the state government to take a call on his plea, but the authorities have so far not told the court what they intend to do.At the last hearing on 19 August, authorities told the court that the Sentence Review Board (SRB), which is examining Singh's plea, was waiting for some more paperwork and sought an adjournment.The two-judge bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Vijay Bishnoi expressed their annoyance at the several adjournments the state had sought in the case and said if the SRB failed to decide Singh's plea by 2 September, the court would. "You take a decision, whichever way you want. If you do not take a decision, then we will."On Wednesday, though, the court did not hear the case. The date for the next hearing is yet to be announced. Reports that Singh may walk free if the state government or the court accept his remission petition have led to some disquiet in India's 30-million Christian community - some of it because of unease over his earlier statements.In his 2000 India Today interview, he said he had "no regrets" and "will never regret" killing Staines' children. "When Hindus die, others don't cry. Why should we weep when others die? Whatever has happened is right. Whatever will happen will also be right."If released from prison, he said, he would "go back to what I have been doing - oppose cow slaughter and conversions"."The government must stop them. If they are not stopped, more people might get killed. Anything can happen," he added.In an article on the Union of Catholic News (UCN) website, human rights and Christian political activist John Dayal wrote recently that remission after decades in jail is "not unusual" in India and "the principle behind it - that punishment should allow for reform and eventual return to society - is humane". But the anxiety among religious minorities in Odisha "is not abstract given the state's history of anti-Christian violence", Dayal points out, citing the Kandhamal riots of 2008, in which dozens were killed and tens of thousands were displaced. "The Staines murders were not an ordinary homicide but a public, theatrical act of terror, intended to be seen and understood as a warning. The killings of Father Arul Doss and Sheikh Rehman extended that same message," he writes."What remains to be seen is not whether Singh will eventually walk free, but how the government conducts itself around that decision...and whether minority communities are given any reassurance," Dayal adds.

schema.headline: Odisha: Why Dara Singh, murderer of Christian missionary Graham Staines and his sons, may walk free in India

title: Nepal intensifies relief and recovery efforts after deadly floods, UN says
description: Nepal is intensifying relief and recovery operations following the catastrophic flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border a week ago, the UN says, eve
body: Nepal is intensifying relief and recovery operations following the catastrophic flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border a week ago, the UN says, even as rescuers scramble to reach anyone who may be alive.For thousands, the priority is delivering aid, recovering loved ones, tracing missing relatives and reunifying separated children, the UN secretary-general's spokesman said.At least 1,114 people have died in Nepal and nearly 4,000 more are missing, according to Nepal's disaster agency. On the Tibetan side, the death toll is 21, with more than 540 people unaccounted for, Chinese state media report.Efforts are continuing to rescue workers, potentially in the hundreds, believed to be trapped in Nepalese hydropower tunnels.A massive flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through a Himalayan valley last Wednesday, wiping out villages. Nearly 12,000 people have since been rescued, according to Nepal's disaster management agency. But thousands more, including hundreds of foreign nationals - from India, the UK,  Australia, the US, Malaysia and more - are still missing. A week on, fears are growing that the death toll will only rise.Chinese rescue teams are continuing to search for more than 500 people missing on the Tibetan side of the border, but they have yet to find survivors at the crossing known as Gyirong Port between Nepal and Tibet.Beijing, which annexed Tibet in the 1950s, tightly controls the region. All information comes from state media and foreign journalists cannot travel there without permission.Rescuers using heavy machinery, working around the clock, have been able to re-open the route to the Gyirong border crossing and clear the road of debris, which will accelerate the search for the missing, Chinese state media said. Rescue operations continue in challenging conditions, and experts from China and India are helping build temporary bridges to reach remote areas. Drones are being deployed over hard-to reach areas to scan for survivors.The UN's Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) says the main challenge is access, with more than 40 bridges destroyed. The most remote communities are relying on army helicopter flights for supplies, and villages are still struggling for fuel and electricity.The full impact of the flood in Tibet is unclear. China has released information through state media outlets showing the devastation around the border, but has given few details about the victims or the impact on local villagers.In Nepal, nearly 3,500 people have been left homeless and displaced in 27 sites - mostly schools, which disrupts education - across the districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa.People packed into overcrowded shelters, contaminated water and damaged health facilities were putting the population at greater risk of disease in the middle of the monsoon season, OCHA said.Nepal's Prime Minister, Balendra Shah, said there was a renewed emphasis on protecting the lives of survivors, providing medical treatment and psychological counselling.Shah told parliament on Wednesday the disaster "snatched away mothers, fathers, sisters, and brothers from us in an instant". But he added "we do not have the luxury of taking a rest simply because our bodies are exhausted. Nor is there time to wail together when our hearts break."He said he had received news at 08:45 local time on 26 August that a flood had hit. Fifteen minutes later, district administrative offices urged people along riverbanks to evacuate, and at 09:35, precautionary warning notices were sent to mobile phones in affected areas.In response to "why there was no timely flood warning", he said the disaster "was beyond predictable forecasts".A new report has said there was evidence of growing instability around the glacier in the days before the collapse. Better early-warning systems could have saved lives, according to experts from the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, the Stimson Centre and China's Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment.Scientists for years have warned of melting ice and permafrost, which is centuries-old frozen soil, in the Himalayas due to climate change.Shah said the event showed the escalating risks facing the Himalayan region due to climate change, adding the time had come to "present a strong case before the international community regarding the disasters we are suffering" as a result."Climate change is a global contribution. Mitigating and managing its impacts is a shared responsibility of the global community," he said.Nepal has declared a disaster in 15 affected areas for three months to provide financial assistance to families of the dead, rescue and relocate the displaced and deploy the army. The Nepalese government and the UN have agreed to launch a four-month humanitarian flash appeal.
